title: Swara Bhasker on Bollywood's Evolution: The Khans, OTT and the Industry's Reckoning
excerpt: In a series of candid interviews, the actor weighs in on Salman Khan's mentorship, streaming's levelling of stardom, the boycott-era slump and the industry's storytelling habits.
body:
• Swara Bhasker says Salman Khan personally mentored her during 2015's Prem Ratan Dhan Payo, coaching her on camera craft, styling and "the psychology of stardom."
  • The actor has repeatedly argued that streaming has "democratised creativity and stardom," opening space for new stories outside the box-office system.
  • Bhasker blames Bollywood's box-office slump on the economic slowdown, COVID-19 and OTT — not just boycott campaigns.
  • Her assessments span the Khans' three-decade dominance and shifting audience tastes.

Swara Bhasker has never treated celebrity as a gag order. In a run of candid interviews — including a recent sit-down that reignited debate about Hindi cinema — the actor has laid out an unusually blunt account of Bollywood's evolution: the three-decade reign of the Khans, streaming as a creative equaliser and an industry rethinking its storytelling.

The Khans and the star machine

Bhasker broke through with Tanu Weds Manu (2011), Raanjhanaa (2013) and Nil Battey Sannata (2016), straddling commercial titles like Prem Ratan Dhan Payo (2015) and Veere Di Wedding (2018), and independent cinema.

On the sets of the 2015 Sooraj Barjatya blockbuster, where she played Salman Khan's sister, the superstar took an unexpected interest in her trajectory. "What surprised me most was how invested Salman was in transforming me," Bhasker said in a recent interview. "He wasn't just focused on his own performance — he was actively thinking about my career trajectory and how to position me as a leading lady." Khan coached her on camera angles and lighting specific to heroines, carrying traditional outfits and screen presence — what she called "the psychology of stardom."

"Working with Salman in a Sooraj Barjatya film was like a masterclass in mainstream cinema."

— Swara Bhasker

Her reading of the star system has long circled around Shah Rukh Khan, Salman Khan and Aamir Khan. "An actor can become a star, but to retain that position like SRK, Salman or Aamir for 25 years is difficult," she said in 2017 — and trade analysts say Hindi cinema still has not built a successor generation.

OTT as the great leveller

Bhasker's most sustained argument concerns streaming. In a 2020 interview with Bollywood Hungama's Subhash K. Jha, she said: "OTT platforms have not only changed content by opening up a space for new stories, new characters and new ideas to be accepted, they have also democratised content. They've democratised creativity and by giving a platform to talented new and old actors OTT has democratised stardom."

Six years on, that readjustment is still underway, with 2026 box-office data showing theatrical revenues increasingly concentrated in a handful of tentpoles.

The boycott debate

When India Today asked her about the 'Boycott Bollywood' campaigns, Bhasker called the attempts to bring the industry down "petty and disgusting," pointing out that it provides livelihoods to thousands. Quoting director Anurag Kashyap, she said the country's economic slump explained part of the downturn — along with COVID-19 and OTT drawing audiences away from theatres. "After the unfortunate and tragic suicide of Sushant, Bollywood has been painted as a really dark place," she said.

A reckoning with her own films

Bhasker has also turned her candour on her own filmography. In a 2025 conversation with Hauterrfly, she revisited the controversy over Raanjhanaa (2013) — criticised for glorifying stalking — admitting she had not seen the problem while making it. "India is full of 'naskatuye aashiq'," she said, arguing that Hindi cinema's biggest hits keep returning to the suffering male hero: "Mardon ki bechargi se zyada profitable art mein kuch nahi hai" — nothing is more profitable in art than stories about victimised men, citing Raanjhanaa, Devdas and Saiyaara.

"OTT platforms have not only changed content by opening up a space for new stories, new characters and new ideas to be accepted, they have also democratised content."

— Swara Bhasker, on streaming

Impact and analysis

Bhasker's position — commercial insider and outspoken outsider — makes her a useful barometer. Her remarks connect the threads of the moment: a concentrated star system struggling to produce new headliners, the streaming correction that rewrote distribution economics and audiences migrating toward southern-language cinema. She has also been open about the personal cost, saying producers have told her she carries "nuisance value" and that her activism cost her work.

Diaspora angle

For diaspora audiences, whose Hindi-film viewing now runs overwhelmingly through streaming, Bhasker's argument that OTT has "democratised stardom" describes how NRIs already experience Bollywood — with smaller films and regional titles a click away from the tentpoles.

What's next

Bhasker is currently seen on the reality show Pati Patni Aur Panga. Whether her political candour continues to limit her casting — a tradeoff she has described as "conscious" — will test how much room the industry genuinely has for dissent.
